quote: every bird has four spectrally distinct cone visual pigments with wavelengths of maximum absorption at long (LWS; lmax 543–571 nm), medium (MWS; lmax 497–510nm), short (SWS; lmax 430–463nm) and extreme short wavelengths (UVS/VS; lmax 362–426nm).

method: microspectrophotometry across species

source.authors: Hart NS
source.title: The visual ecology of avian photoreceptors
source.journal: Progress in Retinal and Eye Research

quote: Where complete data are available, every bird has four spectrally distinct cone visual pigments
note: Four single-cone classes used for colour; double cones and rods besides.

value: double cones serve luminance and movement detection, not wavelength discrimination (limited evidence)
method: review of behavioural and modelling studies

source.authors: Hart NS
source.title: The visual ecology of avian photoreceptors
source.journal: Progress in Retinal and Eye Research

quote: Limited evidence suggests that double cones are not involved in wavelength discrimination under photopic conditions (Maier and Bowmaker, 1993; Vorobyev and Osorio, 1998) but are implicated in movement detection (Cam- penhausen and Kirschfeld, 1998).
note: For the engine: a bird view should drive motion and fine detail from one broad long-wavelength channel, and colour from the four single cones.

value: R-type droplets in LWS single cones cut off below about 570 nm; T-type droplets in UVS/VS cones are transparent from 330 to 800 nm
method: microspectrophotometry

source.authors: Hart NS
source.title: The visual ecology of avian photoreceptors
source.journal: Progress in Retinal and Eye Research

quote: Avian LWS single cones contain an oil droplet (R-type) that cuts off wavelengths below about 570nm and appears red when viewed under the light microscope
note: Second fact from p. 684: T-type droplets show no detectable absorption from at least 330-800 nm.

method: cone counts

source.authors: Hart NS
source.title: The visual ecology of avian photoreceptors
source.journal: Progress in Retinal and Eye Research

quote: the relative proportion of the different cone types in the retina (1:1.9:2.7:2.7 for the UVS, SWS, MWS and LWS single cones, respectively; Hart et al., 2000c).
note: Cone proportions 1:1.9:2.7:2.7 (UVS:SWS:MWS:LWS) set the relative receptor noise in a receptor-noise-limited model. Listed as Parus caeruleus.

method: ocular media transmission: wavelength of 50 percent transmittance

source.journal: Progress in Retinal and Eye Research
